title: An Ice Island as Big as Manhattan Just Broke Off Greenland
gist: A calving event at Greenland's Petermann Glacier released an ice island roughly the size of Manhattan (about 30 square miles, 492 feet thick), the largest Arctic calving since 2020 and the biggest floating ice loss from that glacier in 14 years.

insights.claim: An international research team has monitored Greenland's Petermann Glacier and its extended floating ice tongue for several years, and a newly observed calving event released an ice island of nearly 30 square miles and about 492 feet thick.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, measured data point (size and thickness) for tracking the pace of Arctic ice-tongue disintegration, relevant to sea-level and Arctic ice-loss monitoring.
insights.quote: At an area of nearly 30 square miles and a thickness of around 492 feet, it’s the largest Arctic calving since 2020, and the biggest floating ice loss from this particular glacier in 14 years.

insights.claim: The Petermann Glacier calving event is the largest Arctic calving since 2020 and the biggest floating ice loss from that specific glacier in 14 years.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Establishes this as a notable, above-baseline event against recent Arctic calving history, useful for benchmarking against past ice-loss records.
insights.quote: it’s the largest Arctic calving since 2020, and the biggest floating ice loss from this particular glacier in 14 years

insights.claim: Glaciologist Adam Garbo of the University of Ottawa said Petermann Glacier has long been one of Greenland's largest remaining ice tongues, and that researchers had anticipated this break for years before it finally happened.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Confirms this was a long-anticipated, monitored event rather than a surprise, indicating the scientific community has been tracking Petermann's structural weakening for years.
insights.quote: “Petermann Glacier has long been one of Greenland’s largest remaining ice tongues,” glaciologist Adam Garbo from the University of Ottawa said in a statement. “We’ve anticipated this break for years, and seeing it finally happen is remarkable.”
